utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Inger de Ru, Rafael La Cruz, and Barney Thomas for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Tina Drolec, our new intern Mr. Morrison, my name is Gregor Guy-Smith, and Boris Zorko on behalf of Mr. Perisic. Mr. Zorko will be leading the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will only need a couple of moments to get organised. Your Honours, our next witness is Mr. Drago Covilo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Is Mr. Covilo still coming from the region?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, he is here. I'm waiting for him to appear in the courtroom. There he is, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Covilo.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: My name is Boris Zorko and I'm attorney-at-law, and together with Miss Tina Drolec and Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith I will be representing the Defence for Mr. Perisic. Before. We proceed, we need to bear in mind the fact that the interpreters have to interpret what we say and the transcribers have to record everything, so please pause before answering my question so that everything can be properly recorded.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Can you first state your full name for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: My name is Drago Covilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Give us your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: I was born on the 24th of September, 1946, in Nevesinje, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to be as efficient as possible, I'll present to you -- I'll put to you some of the facts relating to your professional career. Please hear me out and then let me know if the information is correct. You graduated from the military academy in 1968 in the field of communications; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: In 1972 you graduated from the political college, is that right, with an associate degree?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: In 1979, you graduated from the high military academy?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: I don't know if it was in 1979 or 1980, but that's true that around about that time I graduated from the associate degree military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you. After 1979 you were assigned to a communications regiment with the Supreme Command of the Yugoslav People's Army in Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Yes. As I graduated from the post-secondary military academy, I was posted to the communications regiment or regiment of signalmen with the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thereafter you were assigned to the General Staff of the JNA, specifically to the communications administration, and you held the post of a desk officer for communications; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. After awhile with the communications regiment a year or two, I assigned to the General Staff of the JNA with the department of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thereafter you were head of the communications department as well as the department charged with the development of communications?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Yes. For a while I served with the department for the preparation of communications, system for the setup of the communications system. And then as of 1992, I was assigned to the department for the development of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: As of August 1992 through to the end of 1993 you held the post of chief of department for the development and use of the branch of communications with the Army of Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: In 1993 you were assigned to the post of chief of department for operations and staff affairs in the communications sector, or rather, the sector for communications, information technology, and electronic warfare with the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Yes. I don't recall the exact date. I think this was in late 1993 that the secretary for communications, information technology, and electronic warfare was set up. And I was assigned to be the chief of department within that sector and the department was charged with operational and staff affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: You held that post up until 1999 when you became director of the sector for combat preparations with the Ministry of Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Yes. This was in the Ministry of Defence but I was within the PTT of Serbia, post, telecommunications and telegraph. Post, telecommunications and telegraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Covilo. Was it in May of 1992 that you spent a period of time in Bosnia and Herzegovina; and if so, on which duties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: As the Army of Yugoslavia was set up and as a decision was issued to the effect that the JNA units would withdraw from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, sometime in the month of May, I was tasked by the chief of the communications administration with a mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina aimed at providing assistance in the pullout of the JNA units present there. There was a large operational contingent there, part of which was an element of a unit of the Supreme Command, i.e., elements of the communications regiment from Belgrade. My task was to assist in the unhindered departure of men and equipment from Bosnia-Herzegovina to Yugoslavia. Since the civilian communications system had been set up through the node in Mostar because of the operations that were well known, all the PTT lines in Bosnia-Herzegovina were severed. Since I was a communications planner and was quite familiar with the communications setup in all the republics of the former Yugoslavia, one of my basic tasks was to assist in making these communications up and running. Since I knew that the Army of Republika Srpska was being set up in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the main question I put to the chief as soon as he told me that I was to go on a mission there was for how long I was to be in Bosnia-Herzegovina and when was the date of my return planned. I asked this because I knew that individuals who hailed from Bosnia-Herzegovina were given the possibility to stay behind in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you, but it will be very difficult to follow such long answers, so please try and be as concise as possible in your answers.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: And I'll try and be as brief as possible as well.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: In other words, I was given assurances that I would return, and as soon as I completed my mission in early August, the chief the communications administration recalled me to the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Covilo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you, sir, to be saying that you were sent by the JNA to go and set up the communication lines around Mostar which had been cut off, and who were you setting these up for? In other words, for whose benefit were you setting them up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In principle, Mr. President, your understanding is correct. I was supposed to assist in restoring communications lines, PTT systems in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Bileca, Trebinje, Nevesinje, and Gacko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question is, for whose benefit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the benefit of the PTT systems in these areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Let us be quite clear on this issue: The PTT system of the time, was it considered good? It had been considered civilian communications system?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: The PTT system was considered to be a civilian communications system at all times save for the fact that part of these lines could be used for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you. To make the matter quite clear, during your professional career you were a member of which army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Throughout my professional career I was a member of the JNA and subsequently of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Covilo. On your return to the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and bearing in mind the fact that you hail from Bosnia-Herzegovina, were there requests made for your posting to the VRS, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. The Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska did make such requests, and as far as I know, General Mladic himself requested that I be posted there. This because I was deemed by some at the time to be a connoisseur of the communications system and that I would be the man for the job. I had always made it clear that I didn't want to go to the area, that I was a member of the VJ, and my superior officers showed consideration for my views and believed that I should remain a member of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Covilo. Now, your decision or your choice to stay with the Army of Yugoslavia, did it have any negative bearing on you personally?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to be clear, you said your superiors believed that you should remain a member of the Army of Yugoslavia. Are you saying by your next answer that indeed you did remain a member of the Army of Yugoslavia? You were not transferred to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, your duties and obligations, did they change with the establishment of the Army of Yugoslavia; and if so, in what sense?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Your Honour, did they change. Well, partly they did. This was a new army and for the better part of it there was a new system of organisation put in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Covilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to show to the witness Exhibit D200, specifically page 17 in Serbian, and the English translation page 43, doc ID 1D120972. For efficiency of proceeding, I have prepared a binder which I would like to be shown first to the Prosecutor and to be then handed to the witness who will use it during my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means, Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If need be, I can repeat that the English translation has doc ID 1D120972.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, while we are waiting for the English translation, please tell us in simple terms what the main powers of the sector for communications were, that's to say the department you were a member of as of 1992.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: In order for you to fully understand my future evidence, I will tell you how the sector was organised briefly. At the head of the sector, and I'll use an abbreviation, VA, there was the assistant Chief of the General Staff. My department had a role of a staff of an HQ to play for that organ. The sector was an administrative and specialist body of the General Staff tasked with the use and development as well as equipping of the communications systems, IT, and electronic warfare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you, Mr. Covilo. The document that is appearing in the English does not look to me like it's a translation of the document that appears in the B/C/S. I don't whether you can see it, Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting but I might be of assistance. We should be looking at page 43 of the document, where we see the description of the sector we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We now see a document that looks like it could be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Covilo, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I repeat what I just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: No, need, Mr. Covilo. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Thank you. It comprised all of the functions of the directly subordinated organisational units. Each of the administrations had its own component organisational units. In the briefest of terms, what were their obligations? The main principal purpose of the sector was to keep down the manning figures in the administrations and to pool some of these obligations together; financing, providing equipment, mobilisation, personnel related issues, and frequency distribution. I won't elaborate any further but those were the principal duties of the sector for communications, information technology, and electronic activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Covilo. Mr. Covilo, how did the planning work for the communications sector back in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Zorko, the same thing applied to any army throughout the world. The communications sector was planned by communication organs in keeping with their own documents and regulations, specifically, different sets of instructions and rules governing their work. The communications programme would be drafted for each separate command level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Covilo. Were there any differences in terms of the planning process in relation to communications after the VJ had been established?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Nothing particularly noteworthy in terms of differences. The same system was kept. There were some peculiarities that characterised the new system, but nothing real essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Covilo. As far as communications planning is concerned, which is something you mentioned, who was familiar with these plans in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: I will try to provide an accurate answer to this question. In order to do that, I have to point out that in the JNA the division worked as follows: There were two types of communications; operating or stationary communications, and communications at the ready, or on standby. As for operating communications, all of the users were familiar. As for standby communications, only the organs actually drafting those plans were familiar with those.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Covilo. Can you tell us what types of communications existed that were used by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: The same ones as for the JNA. In addition to the basic division that I mentioned in my previous answer, I should add that there was radio relay, there was analogue communication, there was protected communication, wire communication, radio communication, courier communication, and signal communication at lower levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Covilo. You mentioned several different types of communications. Could you please explain in the briefest of terms what each of them mean. What is the exchange of information that these types of communication enable us to have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: The most acceptable answer would be that a line of communication is a line between two persons, between two centres, two towns, two garrisons. The system of communications in the JNA, the VJ, or any other army in the world is not very different from such systems as are used by civilian bodies; it fulfills the basic need for two persons to communicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Covilo. Among other things, you mentioned stationary communications systems. What would that imply?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: A stationary system provides the backbone for the communications system in its entirety. It comprises stationary communications centres and stationary communication hubs. There are external routes between the stationary centres and the stationary hubs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Covilo. When you speak of the stationary communications system, what sort of lines could be established by using this system? What does that mean in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: A stationary communications system is a small PTT centre within a garrison. Depending on a garrison's size, various types of communications were used. For example, you have the town of Bar in Montenegro. There's a battalion there. They have a communications centre that can be accessed by wire alone. For example, Podgorica in Montenegro, there is another communications centre there from which all types of communication lines emanated; radio, wire, courier, and radio relay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, how many units could such a stationary communications centre in the JNA cover?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Your Honours, allow me to use an example. Suppose we have a small PTT centre in the town of Visegrad. It covers all of Visegrad's inhabitants. This is a stationary communications system in the town of Visegrad. It comprises all of the units and institutions located at a point in time within the area covered by that particular garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, let's try to make this as clear as possible. The Zagreb garrison, while the JNA were still around, how many units did that centre cover, communication-wise?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: A garrison was any location at all at which a unit of the JNA were stationed. If this was a battalion, a single battalion, then that's what was covered. If it was some sort of a merged or joint unit, there could have been any number of those; five brigades, six brigades. In larger garrisons such as Podgorica, Montenegro; Sarajevo, Bosnia-Herzegovina; and Nis, Serbia, there were many joint units there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: If my understanding is correct, a garrison like that could establish a communication line to any other garrison throughout the SFRY at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That was the fundamental purpose of the stationary communications system. It enabled communication to any unit and institution throughout the SFRY. For example, you have a garrison in Vipava, Slovenia. One could have unhindered communication to a garrison stationed in Bitola, Macedonia. It wasn't a hot line, as we called it, but one needed an intercession, a mediation, on behalf of other intermediary communications centres that lay between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, were all of the garrisons throughout the former JNA linked up or connected in the same way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Yes. If you consider my previous answers, you could tell there were a number of, peculiarities there. Smaller garrisons had one type of communications alone and larger garrisons had several different types of communication that were available to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: You mentioned something you called the stationary communication hub [Realtime transcript read in error "had you been"]. Can you please try to explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Your Honours, in one of my previous answers I said that the stationary system provided the background to the communications system in its entirety. This was a true backbone, this communication hub. The stationary communication hub is normally an installation built at some sort of elevation. From there, one establishes several radio relay lines and a smaller number of radio lines. The stationary hubs would normally be found in underground installations. The only thing that was above the ground were the antennae. Likewise at a stationary communications hub, in addition to establishing radio relay lines, one performed the commutation; that is, there was a switchboard there for different communication lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt my learned friend. There's, at page 14, line 1, just a correction required to the transcript. The question at the moment as recorded reads: "You mentioned something called a stationary communication had you been," and obviously it's "stationary communication hub," and that needs to be reflected, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm trying to look at page 14, line 1. I'm not seeing what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, the question actually begins page 13, line 25: "You mentioned something called the stationary communication --" and what should follow is the word "hub."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thomas. Yes. Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you also to my learned friends. I myself have a point to raise about the transcript. [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. What I was hearing is quiet now. Can you raise your point, Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Likewise a small intervention. Page 14, lines 9 and 10. The transcript reflects something the witness didn't actually say, "Han Pijesak," whereas it should be "hub." Because that's what the witness was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The name "Han Pijesak" should come out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, who was it that manned those stationary communications centres? Who was in charge of operating those centres on the ground?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Again I have to go back to something that I have often been pointing out. It depends on the centre's size. If we are talking about the relatively small communications centre with battalions there, you would have ordinary private soldiers doing their regular military term manning those. If you look at a centre of an average size, normally one would have civilians serving in the JNA and any given number of active duty officers manning those centres. It is noteworthy that the civilians normally came from the area in which the communications centre was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Covilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have OTP Exhibit P469 brought up on our screens. This is a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, you won't find this map in your binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we go to that map, Mr. Zorko, I'm advised that this document that's on the screen is not part of the original document, and whether you -- what would you like to do with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since D200 was MFI'd at one point in time, we shall in due course be tendering it. Nevertheless, I do hope that we can work with our colleagues from the OTP to see whether there might be any objections against the admission of this document. We are still waiting to see whether the translation is accurate and are content to leave it as an MFI for the time being. We need a full translation for this document to be revised. This is quite a substantial, comprehensive document. For the time being, we are happy to leave it as it is. In due course we shall be asking for that document and a number of other documents to be properly admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you correct me, this D200 is marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But [Overlapping speakers] ... only [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What you want to do is to add this page to the pages that are marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Pending that translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, I'm probably creating some confusion in relation to this document. It has been used with certain witnesses, some portions of it were. We have submitted it to be fully translated and the translation that you have been looking at is the full translation. Therefore, we shall be asking to have the full translation cross-referenced to the original document that runs into a total of 29 pages, the original being in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Zorko, you are interpreted as having said "We have submitted it to be fully translated and the translation that you have been looking at is the full translation." Now it can't be, we've been looking at one page and you are telling us that the whole thing is about, what, 29 pages or even more. It does seem as if some pages have been admitted but marked for identification, and it seems to me that the procedure that we would like to follow is to say that the page that we saw today be added to the marked -- to the pages that are marked for identification. And as and when you use the pages that have not been marked so will you be asking that they be added to those.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite right, Your Honour. I do apologise for unnecessarily causing confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not a problem. Not a problem. Okay. Then yes, this page then will be added to the marked for identification part of D200. We may call P469 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, you have a map before you. Could we have usher's assistance so that you may mark on this map the location of the place that you called the stationary communications hub or the backbone of the communications system, to the best of your recollection, in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Zorko, the map is so small that I'm really unable to get my bearings here. I don't even see the territory of the former SFRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My concern, Mr. Zorko, is that you are -- again you are interpreted as asking the witness to mark it to the best of his recollection in Croatia. The map we have before us looks like a middle of a town, not a middle of a country. Unless you tell me what town this is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, apologies on behalf of the Registry as the wrong document was shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, you should be able to see a map now. It's perhaps not the most visible of maps and I'm not asking for absolute precision on your part. What I would like you to do is to mark in Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the FRY the location of the stationary communications hubs as you recall them.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Zorko, I will do my best, but please do understand that it's been 20 years since I last dealt with the system. At any rate, I will do this to the best of my recollection, but don't hold it against me if I omit to mark any of the hubs or mismark them. Let's start from Croatia, from numbers 1 onwards, and I'm not sure that it's going to be the exact location because I can't see it correctly but I'll say the name of the location. One of them was Sunj; number 2 is Papuk; 3, Drinska Gora; 4, Petrova Gora; 5, Moslavacka Gora; 6, Licka Pljesevica; 7, Celavac; 8, Kozjak. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, as far as I can remember, 9, Veliki Zep; 10, Bjelasnica; 11, Borasnica; 12, Velez; 13, Kmur; 14, Kozara; 15, Vitorog; 16, Majevica; 17, Cvrsnica; and 18 Klekovaca, I believe. In Serbia, let's start from number 20, Fruska Gora; 21, Avala; 22, Cer; 23, Jagodnja; 24, Cigota; 25, Strazbenica; 26, Maljen; 27, Jastrebac. In Kosovo, number 28, Butovacki Breg; and 29, Mokra Gora. And I believe I forget to mark Crni Vrh. This is roughly the communications hubs that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please save the marked map. Let me just state that number 6 relates to a communications hub you said was in Croatia. Can you please confirm if that's correct or not.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Licka Pljesevica, yes, it's in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: That's number 6?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Yes, Licka Pljesevica was in Croatia. Yes, apologies, pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Drago, please do not make any additional markings on the map because we want to save it as it is now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we save it, I'm not quite sure that later when we look at the map we will be able to recognise 14, 15, and 25 -- oops, it's all gone. Mr. Registrar. I was going to ask whether there was a way in which, one, we could delete only that 6 that was inside Bosnia-Herzegovina and perhaps also try to rewrite 14, 15, and 25 so that it's readable later when we do read it. Mr. Registrar assures me that he will be able to bring it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar has brought back the map as marked, but before the correction, before the shifting of the 6 out of BiH into Croatia. Now, Mr. Covilo, you corrected yourself at number 6. You remember, you took out number 6 out of Bosnia-Herzegovina and put it into Croatia because, according to your testimony, it was supposed to be in Croatia. Can you do that again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can, but please bear in mind that I did not place the numbers on the exact locations because I can't see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, we understand that, Mr. Covilo. Now, Mr. Registrar, is it possible for the witness to correct 14, 15, and 25 without erasing the whole thing? Are you able to help him there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm told that cannot happen. We'll have to accept it as it is. Are you tendering that? Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, though it should be said for the transcript that we have two number 6 and that the one to the left is in the Republic of Croatia, and that number 14 looks like 154 in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's why I asked if that could be corrected. Mr. Covilo, can you strike off the 6 that's inside Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I'm told the only amendment that you can do to 14 and 15 is to strike them out and write the correct numbers, but if you try to erase them, you are going to erase all of the numbers. Now, Mr. Covilo, do you still see where you wrote number 14?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's wrong; it says 154.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. Can you strike that out and try to write 14 neatly next to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, do you see what is 15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What does it look like to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5 is not properly written. Can I correct it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please do. Thank you. I'm trying to look for number 25 because I thought I had a similar problem with it. Yes, I do. It looks like an incomplete 28 just below 27. No, below 24, below 24.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Strazbenica. Can I correct it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you correct it, please. Good. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just remembered that I forgot the hub in Serbia called Kopaonik, which is very important. Can I please mark it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please mark it. We already have a 30, Mr. Covilo. Could you make that a 31?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It must now look like 301. Thank you so much. Right. Yes, Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Let's try and proceed with the map. I can see that Mr. Barney [Realtime transcript read in error "Tolimir"] is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I don't know if we are at the point yet where this image is going to be tendered. Just to make matters a little more confusing, at page 19, line 9, Mr. Covilo had very helpfully marked number 29, Mokra Gora, and then he says at line 9, "I believe I forgot to mark Crni Vrh." And I see on the map a number 30 has been entered on the map but it's not clear from the transcript whether Crni Vrh has actually been marked on the map as number 30 or not. I'm just lost as to whether number 30 actually is Crni Vrh and whether Crni Vrh has actually been recorded on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to help us, Mr. Covilo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really don't remember the time-line. I can tell you that Fruska Gora is 20, Avala is 21, Cer is 22, et cetera. So I know that I did say Crni Vrh but I'm not sure which number I correlated it to. It might be 30 or 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said page, Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Page 19, line 9, sir. Perhaps I could suggest that to avoid all doubt we simply give Crni Vrh a number 32 now. We just put it on the map now, number 32, and then it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to mark Crni Vrh now, Mr. Covilo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since it's quite occupied, the place here, I'm going to place it elsewhere. There, 32, Crni Vrh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We are not that lucky with the technology today. Let's correct the transcript, line 22 -- or rather page 22, line 9, I said that I saw Mr. Thomas on his feet and Mr. Tolimir's name can be read in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 22, line 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, I do see Mr. Tolimir. You wanted to say Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see him at the movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is duly corrected. Okay. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, now that you've marked these stationary communications hubs, can you tell us where the communications system was at its densest when we are talking about former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Zorko, let me again place a caveat and say that I may have omitted some of the hubs, I don't recall them. Let me tell you that the communications system was best developed in the central part of the country, that's to say in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Serbia, and it was somewhat poorer in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Covilo. The stationary communications hubs, as they were dispersed across the territory, did they, in view of their locations, best serve their role?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if you could put it that way, but they did make possible unhindered communication in these republics with the units that had the requisite operational equipment. If I may, let me say that there were at least three to four radio relay routes from each of these hubs and that all of these hubs were interconnected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, if my understanding is correct, in order for these stationary hubs to have mutual communication in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was it necessary for them to resort to the hubs in Serbia, or rather, in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Zorko, in order for a communications to exist between two participants, there have to be two participants at two ends, so each of these hubs could communicate with either of the others. There was no need for them in Bosnia to communicate with Serbia if they did not want to or if this was not planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Was a system like this in place between 1993 and 1995 as well as later?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Following the withdrawal of the JNA units, most of the stationary communication hubs and communications centres remained outside Serbia. The damage to the communication lines varied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Covilo. You also mentioned standby communications, talking about the overall infrastructure. Can you explain what that means, standby communication?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: I'll try to be as brief as possible. We said that operating communication lines were communication lines for peacetime conditions. Standby communication lines are used when units go to certain areas based on their deployment plans. This may be a situation of combat or an emergency, such as an earthquake, floods, or anything like that. That type is used whenever a unit leaves its peacetime assignment area. Communication lines are organised depending on a unit's level from a facility where their command is located, or mobile communication vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Is there any connection between these and the stationary communication hubs? Can this in any way affect the quality or indeed the density of communication lines?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: There is a relation between the two, that much is certain. The stationary communications system is part of this system, it is a component of this system. A certain number of channels is only ever used for operative units leaving their peacetime locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Covilo. Could you please in the briefest of terms also explain what you mean by a mobile communications centre.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: A mobile communications centre is a centre normally set up in an open area, on open ground, including communication units and equipment borne by a transport vehicle, or mounted on a transport vehicle. This begins at battalion level and goes all the way up to the Supreme Command level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another small intervention. Page 25, line 12, the witness mentioned that there were connections between stationary communication hubs and mobile communications centres. That was not recorded. Page 25, line 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zorko. Where you see that little cap, the stenographer denotes that she is going to check that during the break because she missed that and she's trying to keep up pace with us, so it will be checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now moving on to standby and mobile communication hubs, what do you want to do with this exhibit on the screen? Those are stationary ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point in time, I would like to have this admitted into evidence and marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D468 [Realtime transcript read in error "D648], this final marking on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, what exactly are command facilities and were there any in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Command facilities or installations are locations or buildings from which certain groups exercise command over units subordinated to them. A command facility or installation would normally be a fortified one, very often an underground facility, where communications centres were on standby. Normally it was the Supreme Command as well as certain military district command that had certain facilities and installations. If memory serves, in the case of the Zagreb military district, there was a command post that was partially equipped, and this command post was at Sl unj. As for the Sarajevo military district, this command post was somewhere in the broader area of Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we lose this page, I note that at page 26 line 15 that exhibit has been given D648 instead of D468. Let's just make sure we correct that. Okay. Thank you, Mr. Zorko, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, what about the Supreme Command of the JNA; did it have one or several command posts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: The Supreme Command, as the highest-ranking body in the military forces of the country, had a number of different command posts. Its principal command post was in the general Belgrade area. It was a fortified underground installation. The next command post was in the general Konjic area in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Likewise, this was a fully equipped and fully fortified underground installation. There was a reserve command post too in the Gorazde area. Another underground facility but only partially equipped and fortified. There was also a rear command post in the general Sarajevo area, yet another underground facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, we have all these command posts, what were the links between these? What sort of communications system did they have, and was there communication between these command posts and other units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Zorko, I'm somewhat worried that I might make this a little too meticulous and detailed. I'll try to be as succinct as I can. As I said, most of those installations had a full set of communications equipment. For example, the one in Belgrade, in Konjic, in part also the one in Sarajevo, those were fully equipped, including standby communications equipment, which means that the systems could be operated at any point in time and lines could be established and used by the relevant command. These communication lines were established to lead to each and every group in all of the military districts and there were also links connecting the command posts between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I note the time. This might be a good time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, you are aware of the JNA withdrawal which took place during a certain period of time and the latter formation of the VJ. Can you tell us what happened in terms of the communications structure as it existed in the JNA once it withdrew?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Zorko, in some of my previous answers, I stated that the stationary communication hubs for the most part were located in underground facilities and that the stationary communications centres were located in the various garrisons representing the peacetime locations of institutions and units. When JNA units withdrew, in most of the cases communications equipment remained in those stationary centres. As for the hubs, the stationary hubs, the equipment sustained greater or lesser damage after the withdrawal of some parts of the equipment. The stationary centres and hubs remained basically as such in the locations where they had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Covilo. What happened with the equipment, communications equipment, which was not in the stationary hubs and centres?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: When the JNA units withdrew, a certain amount of equipment was withdrawn as well, especially regarding the mobile communications centre as well as some equipment from the stationary communications centres. However, most of the equipment remained in the locations where the JNA had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Covilo. To your knowledge, who made use of the existing infrastructure and systems you mentioned once the JNA withdrew?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: To my knowledge, it would be difficult to answer, but it is my guess that if most of the equipment remained, that equipment was then used by the newly-established armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened with the PTT communications system. Was it still used for civilian purposes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Each of the republics had an autonomous PTT system in place. After our withdrawal, we no longer received information about those, but I presume those systems were used for the needs of the population in those republics, as well as partially, and I presume that, for the needs of the newly-created armies in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, what happened with the stationary communications centre in Sarajevo, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: The stationary communications centre in Sarajevo was an enormous one, given that it was centrally located in the country. I told you that it even had a command post. Sarajevo is a specific city with a large military presence, and in that single garrison there were several communications centres. As far as I know, those centres remained in operation to the extent possible. As far as I know, after the problems the JNA had withdrawing its units from Sarajevo, it no longer had any influence on the fate of those stationary communications centres because, as we could see from the media, the JNA withdrawal from Sarajevo was a difficult one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Do you know who used the Sarajevo stationary centre, which army, that is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say since I was not familiar with the disposition of forces in Sarajevo. Probably the Muslim side used it as well as the Serb side in certain parts, but I can't be any more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of everything you have said so far, did the JNA infrastructure and communications system -- could it enable the functioning of an independent autonomous communications system in the newly-created republics? Specifically I have in mind the armed forces of Croatia, Slovenia, the Serb army of the Krajina, the VRS, and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Zorko, it is very difficult to give you a specific detailed answer, but when we were marking the stationary communications centres, we also mentioned there was a great many of them, and given that, I can tell you with a high degree of certainty that the existing communications system in Bosnia-Herzegovina was well developed, including the PTT system, to the extent which made all of the newly-formed armed forces with certain changes in terms of organisation, it made it all possible for the armies to use those systems. The situation in the area of the Serb Krajina was slightly worse because there were fewer stationary communications centres because the number of JNA units which had been stationed there was less. As regards Croatia, it had a sufficient number of stationary hubs and centres. In Slovenia, Svetigora, Krhin, and Bos [phoen] were the three stationary communications centres, and in terms of Slovenia's size, I believe it was sufficient for the armed forces of Slovenia, with certain corrections and additions to the communications centres, could use the existing infrastructure to set up their own communications system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Covilo. When you marked the stationary communication hubs, and that was on page 24 and lines 9 to 17, I asked you about the extent of your knowledge, and I have a few more questions about the system as it existed in the JNA. Did the VRS have to use the stationary hubs in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in order to have a functioning communications system? And I would kindly ask to you speak slowly so that everything is reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: The number of hubs depends on the lie of land and whether the facilities in question can be seen from the next such facility, as well as whether the equipment located there was sufficient in any case. The distance between two such hubs was not supposed to exceed 50 kilometres. Each hub was independent and had two, three, or more radio relay routes. All of the hubs together comprised the network and each of them was autonomous. As for any changes in the system, one needed to have a clear view of the next facility and the distance should not have been greater than 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, I'd like to correct line 31 [as interpreted]. The question was whether the Army of Republika Srpska had to use the stationary hubs in the FRY in order to have a functioning communications system. It is page 31, line 21. I will try to be more specific, Mr. Covilo, and if possible, please answer with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: No. The Army of Republika Srpska did not have to rely on the stationary communication hubs in the FRY in order to have a functioning communications system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Covilo. Once the JNA withdrew its units, given the structure you described, did such a complex infrastructure enable the communication of the garrisons, for example, in Zagreb and Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: I will go back to the maxim stating that if there is going to be any communication, one needs to have two participants. In order to have a communication line between Zagreb and Belgrade, one needs to have a functioning communications system in place and there must be a will, of course, on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: I'll try to be even more specific, Mr. Covilo: Did such communication exist during a certain period of time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Can you tell us when exactly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: When JNA units were still in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because of the well-known developments in Croatia, even the PTT communications system was disrupted. International forces also invested great effort in order to achieve a truce in that area. In view of all that, there was a need for a meeting between representatives of Yugoslavia and Croatia. As far as I recall, that meeting actually took place in Bosanski Brod in mid- or late 1991. It was attended by a number of FRY representatives, such as the representatives of the federal telecommunications ministry, the representatives of the PTT, and of the army. I represented the army on behalf of the communications administration. On the Croatian side there was the chief of communications of the Croatian army, Mr. Sisper [phoen] and a PTT representative. It took place under the auspices of a number of international representatives who wanted us to agree on the establishment of a communications system in order to ensure that the truce agreement was abided by, and it was a topical issue at the time. The PTT service on both sides, given that the PTT communications system was disrupted, required that it be re-established. At that meeting, no final agreement was reached. It was agreed, though, that the implementation of that task was to be agreed upon during a next meeting or a set of meetings which were supposed to take place in Croatian territory. Specifically, Zadar was mentioned as well as Pecu, or Pec, in Hungary. The second meeting followed closely behind and the teams on both sides were basically the same. That meeting took place in Slavonski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to interrupt you because the answer is getting very long. What was the final result of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: The final result was the PTT sides agreed to try to get the disrupted communications systems back up and running. As far as I remember, that was the last time it ever got disrupted. As far as the army is concerned, there was now a direct line between the operations centre of the Main Staff of Croatia's army and the operations centre of the General Staff. Likewise, approval was granted to lower-ranking subordinate commands to establish communication lines to their neighbours. The same thing applied to the JNA, which was still in the area, and the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, what became of the communications system in the JNA following its withdrawal and the establishment of the VJ? Did it now set up an independent and autonomous communications system? What exactly was the case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Indeed, the VJ, in order to meet its own needs, set up an autonomous and independent communications system. For that purpose, it used the existing infrastructure and made some minor additions. They formed all of the communications centres in all the newly established garrisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, intervention. Page 35, line 4, it should be "formed" and not "informed."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, were any communication lines set up between the VJ and the armed forces of any of the neighbouring countries, as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Yes. Although at the time I was no longer working in the communications field. I am, however, aware of that, and that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter Defence document 00503, could that be brought up on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Should there been extension D?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 00503D. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, have a look, please. Could you please pay close attention to paragraph 1. There is mention there of establishing a direct communication line between the Hungarian anti-aircraft Defence operation centre and the operation centre in Novi Sad. Would that be consistent with the kind of communication lines that you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was necessary for both sides to be able to use their air force with no hindrance. I remember that there was a communication line established between the VJ and Hungary so that they could each announce flights to the other side and avoid any violations of each other's air-space.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move that this document be exhibited, please, and could we have a number for it, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D469. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, apart from this example involving Hungary, did the VJ establish any contacts with the armed forces of foreign countries in the sense of promoting an already-existing communications system?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Of course it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Could you please elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: This applies to any country in the world. The consequences of operations such as these would have led to certain results, let alone Yugoslavia given the stage of development it had reached by this point. It was necessary to improve our credibility in the world and also to organise a more effective system through the VJ. In my case it had to do with the communications system. As far as that is concerned, I know that we organised visits to the armed forces of Romania, Greece, Egypt, Israel, the purpose being to exchange our experiences and to enhance our communications system and command and information systems. If I may just digress. There was a very fruitful collaboration with Romania and that continued. As far as I remember, a year or two ago we had a joint drill that was held and communications centres were jointly set up by the telecommunication units from Romania and Yugoslavia; that is, Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Covilo. Following the establishment of the VJ, were there any organisational changes that occurred in terms of how the communications system worked in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: The army was established and underwent a transformation. The two processes were mutually dependent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer. I think there is a problem here. Could you please repeat. I think there's a problem here.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: My answer was the VJ was established and its transformation began. Of course, once the transformation was underway, one needed to also transform the communications system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: What exactly did this transformation of the communications system imply?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Above all, the transformation implied new communications being established in the newly-established garrisons. As well as implementation of new instructions and rules that concerned this organisation. Perhaps I should also say that organisational informational changes were also made to communications units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Defence 65 ter Exhibit 01057D. I think it is page 3 in the B/C/S, or perhaps we should remain on page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Item 3, Mr. Covilo, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Could you please comment briefly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: This is a very specific answer to the previous question. There were some changes that occurred and, because of these changes, the army had to adapt. That applied to communications units as well. The training centre EI 5 for electronic surveillance and anti-electronic activities was established. This shows that the army had limited resources and that this was established at the expense of other structures. Paragraph 2. The stationary communication hubs were to be kept under the jurisdiction of the communications administration. Throughout that period in time a special centre was set up, the 235th communications centre, which now unified all of the communications centres in the FRY. This was also the one major organisational informational change that occurred to the structure of communications units throughout the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, let me ask you a simple question: Does that mean that the transformation or the establishment of the VJ caused new structures to arise in terms of what type of communications system was being used for the VJ's purposes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Yes, new structures, needless to say, nevertheless using an already existing infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Mr. Covilo, you say there existed a very elaborate communications system in the former Yugoslavia. Given the elaborate nature of this system, was there any form of protection in the VJ that was used to protect the system?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Let me say at the outset that I'm no specialist in encryption myself. As a communications planner, I had to know what routes were to be protected by what means. The JNA communications system was protected by a written unspoken protection system at lower tactical levels and as far as general command documents were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: You mentioned the JNA in your answer, Mr. Covilo, and I want to know about the VJ. Was there a protection or encryption system in the VJ, and did you mean the VJ and said the JNA? Did you perhaps misspeak?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: The principle was similar, nevertheless there were some peculiarities. This is a very peculiar field. Each army has peculiar methods of protection. It was by default that once the army had been established there had to be some sort of discontinuity in relation to the previous protection system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Mr. Covilo, while you were working on the General Staff of the VJ, did you know that demands were being made by the Serbian Army of Krajina and the VRS in relation to certain pieces of communication equipment in the VJ's possession?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Zorko. Given that the fact that I attended some collegium meetings of the assistant commander of the General Staff for communications, information technology and electronic activity, the meeting also attended by heads of administrations, as a tactical agent, I know that certain requests were made for certain equipment above all certain pieces of communication equipment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, for the purposes of the transcript, could you please slow down a little. We are having some trouble recording what you are saying, therefore please bear in mind the pace of your answers.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown OTP Exhibit P1812.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you call that one, Mr. Zorko, what do you intend doing with 1057D?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I do move that this document be exhibited. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D470. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zorko. Now, what do you want to call, Mr. Zorko?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, OTP Exhibit P1812.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, have a look, please, and tell us what sort of equipment it talks about. Could you briefly explain what type of equipment we are looking at here.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Zorko, this is one of the documents where certain pieces of equipment were approved. As far as I can tell, these are types of equipment for the most part no longer being used by the VJ. The first one is a radio device, AN/GRC-9, it's an old American radio used at battalion and platoon level. And no longer used in the VJ. RUP-12 was used in the VJ. Radio device PRC-147, same purpose as the first one, AN/GRC-9, for the most part no longer used in the VJ. Telephone PTI-49, that's an old telephone first produced in 1949. It was superseded by M-63. I'm not aware of a single instance of this type of phone being used by the VJ. The telephone switchboard, there were newer types, IT C-10, I don't know if it was used by the VJ, but I don't think so. The PTK cable cord was used, the cord reel as well. UN AF device 11, 12, 13, 14, old devices used for permanent air routes. I can't say with certainty whether these were used or not, but I think not, not in the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Covilo. Can the witness please be shown Exhibit P1813.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, take a look at the document and I'll ask for your comments on the equipment contained therein.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Yes. The situation is similar to the one in the earlier document. For the most part these are outdated devices that were used rarely or not at all in that the last device listed here are UFM-200 is a device that was used in the VJ but there was a shortage of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Somehow I'm getting lost. Some names are being called which I don't see on the screen. Like this very last one, UFM-200. Am I looking at the right document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, Your Honour, this is on page 2 of the English version. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, generally speaking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. Zorko. Even on page 2 we don't see UFM-200, we see RRU FM-12. This has been even the previous document I had that problem, but I let it pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, please have a look at the last item listed in the document before you. Can you please repeat your answer in reference to that device. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: This is the radio relay device FM-200. RRU-800 is the one that falls into the same category. This device was used for protected radio relay lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: I do see that there's a difference between the two versions. The English translation states "FM-12" in the last line, whereas the original text in the B/C/S reads "FM-200," and it says at the very end "two pieces." So there's an error in the translation there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In fact, as I say, I had the same problem with P1812. So I would request that those two exhibits be checked, the translations be checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm advised that they are MFI'd pending correct translations, both of them. Maybe when you call them up, call them MFI so that we know what is MFI'd and what is not MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, if any requests came from the Serbian Army of Krajina or the VRS to your administration, what sort of response was there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Let me just correct you, Mr. Zorko, that I was in the department for communications, IT, and electronic warfare and --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the requests mostly came from heads of administration --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I do not believe, sir, that my learned friend has laid a foundation for that question. He asked Mr. Covilo about requests from the VRS and SVK, and Mr. Covilo said that, on the basis of collegium meetings that he was able to attend, he was aware of some requests. So unless he is able to lay a fuller foundation, he cannot put to Mr. Covilo on the basis of the existing foundation what the general practice may or may not have been, because as I understand Mr. Covilo's testimony, it is that his knowledge of this comes from the isolated collegium sessions that he attended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, I will take this from a different angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, how often did the collegiums you referred to meet?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Once a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Did you attend these collegium meetings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Yes, I attended them at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Did the collegium meetings discuss, among other things, the issue of requests for material assistance coming from the SVK and VRS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Yes, whenever there were any such requests to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's fine. That's sufficient foundation for me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank my learned friend. Thank you, Your Honours. Can the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit P874.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it MFI or is it admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit, if I may be of some assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Covilo, take a look at the document. Can you give us your comments which have to do with my earlier question; i.e., what was the prevalent view that your administration or actually your sector took in relation to such requests?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Zorko, I will give you the briefest of answers. The position that the sector took was to approve such requests restrictively insofar as there were assets available within the VJ. Specifically, in this particular case in point we can see that the tactical agents, i.e., the chief of the administration, is directly addressing the office of the chief and informs them that it was not possible to meet the request. In this particular instance, this request was not discussed at the collegium meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Covilo, but there's a problem with the transcript again and could you repeat your answer. Because I think there's a sentence that needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Zorko, the position of the sector for communications, IT, and electronic warfare was to grant these assets, to approve these requests restrictively. This because the VJ did not have assets in stock and the prevalent practice was that such assets were not purchased or provided. As I said, in this particular piece of evidence, as you call it, we can see that, probably for reasons of urgency, the tactical agent concerned is directly addressing the office of the Chief of the General Staff, informing him that he was unable to grant the requested assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Covilo. What does maintenance of communication devices in the VJ imply?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Maintenance of all assets, and particularly those that were in use by various units, implied that such assets should be kept operational at all times, and this falls within the purview of the technical administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Maintenance of communications assets in the VJ, was it subject to some sort of standard procedure as to how it was dealt with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Well, yes. All the armies have a standard procedure in place for that. From the duties to be discharged by those operating the devices, they need to check whether the assets are in order, all the way through to the bodies that are set up which contain experts who are there to make sure that the equipment is in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Is it an activity of any continuity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: Of course it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Does maintaining communications assets in the VJ refer to all the communications equipment held by that army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO COVILO
utterances.text: All the material and technical equipment, including the communications assets, according to the instructions issued by the technical administration, do have to be checked periodically. I don't know what the period is.
